jamb-chemistry-bank-0158.explanation: The outer configuration is 3s² 3p⁵ (7 valence electrons), characteristic of Group 17 (halogens).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0159.explanation: A large electronegativity difference (about 1.7 or greater) indicates electron transfer, hence ionic bonding.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0160.explanation: Atomic number 27 gives 27 protons. Neutrons = 60 − 27 = 33. For a neutral atom, electrons = protons = 27.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0161.explanation: X-ray diffraction is used to study structures/arrangements in large molecules and crystalline materials.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0163.explanation: Nitrogen from air contains traces of heavier noble gases (especially argon), increasing its density.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0164.explanation: Temporary hardness is due to calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates, removable by boiling.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0165.explanation: Efflorescence is the loss of water of crystallization by hydrated salts on exposure to air.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0166.explanation: A liquid dispersed in another liquid forms an emulsion (e.g., milk).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0167.explanation: Preventing pollution at source by treating wastes to harmless products before discharge is the most direct and effective control method among the options.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0168.explanation: Basicity is the number of replaceable (ionizable) hydrogen ions per molecule of acid. Ethanoic acid has one ionizable H in the -COOH group.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0169.explanation: Litmus is purple at neutral pH (about 7).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0170.explanation: By definition, text{pH} = -log₁₀[text{H}^+], equivalently log₁₀(frac{1}{[text{H}^+]}). The option using [text{H}₃text{O}^+] matches this.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0171.explanation: A salt that turns blue litmus red is acidic. Potassium hydrogen tetraoxosulphate is an acid salt (contains replaceable H), giving an acidic solution.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0172.explanation: The reducing agent is Zn. Zn goes from 0 in Zn(s) to +2 in ZnSO4.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0173.explanation: Oxidizing agent is reduced. Hydrogen in H2O goes from +1 to 0 in H2 (reduction), so H2O is the oxidizing agent.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0175.explanation: Copper is deposited from text{Cu}²⁺: 1 mol Cu needs 2 mol electrons = 2F. For 0.25 mol Cu, faradays needed = 0.25× 2 = 0.50F. That corresponds to option D, not A.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0176.explanation: In the energy profile, Z is shown as the vertical difference between the energy level of reactants (A+B) and products (C+D). That vertical change corresponds to the enthalpy change (heat of reaction, Δ H).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0177.explanation: Use Δ G = Δ H - TΔ S. T = 25 + 273 = 298 text{K}. So Δ H = Δ G + TΔ S = -899 + 298× 10 = -899 + 2980 = 2081 text{J mol}⁻¹. This matches option A, not D.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0178.explanation: A very large equilibrium constant means equilibrium lies far to the product side, giving maximum yield of products.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0179.explanation: Rate of reaction is defined as change in concentration per unit time.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0180.explanation: Increasing [text{H}^+] adds a product; by Le Châtelier’s principle the equilibrium shifts left to consume excess text{H}^+, forming more dichromate.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0181.explanation: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Magnesium is above hydrogen; copper and gold are below, and lead is often protected by insoluble PbSO4.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0182.explanation: Concentrated text{H}₂text{SO}₄ is a strong dehydrating agent used to remove water vapour, thus drying the gas.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0183.explanation: In chlorine preparation, hydrogen chloride is a common impurity. Passing the gas through water removes HCl because it is very soluble, while chlorine is less soluble.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0184.explanation: Fluorine is extremely reactive and quickly forms compounds (fluorides), so it is not found free in nature.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0185.explanation: Chlorine is liberated at the anode and platinum is used because it is resistant to attack by chlorine.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0186.explanation: Calcium ions give a brick-red (orange-red) flame in flame tests.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0187.explanation: In the electrolysis of molten CaCl2, calcium metal is deposited at the cathode; iron/steel is commonly used as the cathode material in such setups (graphite is typically an anode).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0188.explanation: Pb(OH)2 forms a white precipitate that is insoluble in excess NaOH under typical qualitative analysis conditions. (Zn(OH)2 and Al(OH)3 dissolve in excess NaOH.)

jamb-chemistry-bank-0189.explanation: Haloalkanes are derived from alkanes (text{C}_ntext{H}₂n₊₂) by replacing one H with X, giving text{C}_ntext{H}₂n₊₁text{X}.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0190.explanation: The parent chain is butanol with the -OH given the lowest possible number (butan-1-ol). Numbering from the OH end gives Cl at C2 and Br at C3. Substituents are listed alphabetically: bromo before chloro, giving 3-bromo-2-chlorobutanol.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0191.explanation: Soap production (saponification of fats/oils) produces glycerol as the alcohol by-product.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0193.explanation: Ethyne is stored dissolved in acetone (propanone) in cylinders to reduce explosion risk.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0194.explanation: Perspex (PMMA) is a transparent, tough plastic used for lenses and light covers such as car rear lights.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0195.explanation: Acid (H+) catalyzes ester hydrolysis by lowering activation energy, increasing reaction rate without changing equilibrium position.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0196.explanation: Vapour density 39 implies molar mass M = 2× 39 = 78. Empirical mass of CH is 12+1 = 13. Multiplier = (78)/(13) = 6. Molecular formula = (text{CH})₆ = text{C}₆text{H}₆.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0197.explanation: Expanded polystyrene foam cushions shocks because it is easily compressed, absorbing impact energy to protect fragile objects.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0198.explanation: Catalytic reforming converts straight-chain hydrocarbons into branched/cyclic/aromatic hydrocarbons, increasing octane number.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0199.explanation: Diesel (gas oil) is commonly used as fuel for industrial heating and furnaces compared with gasoline (motor fuel) and lubricating oil (non-fuel use).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0200.explanation: The header on the page clearly states "PAPER TYPE: I".

jamb-chemistry-bank-0247.explanation: The header on the page states "PAPER TYPE: RED".

jamb-chemistry-bank-0201.explanation: Impurities disrupt the crystal lattice, causing melting point depression (lower melting point).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0202.explanation: Reaction: 2text{C} + text{O}₂ arrow 2text{CO}. Gas volumes at same conditions follow mole ratios: 1 volume of text{O}₂ produces 2 volumes of CO. Thus 10 text{dm}³ text{O}₂ produces 20 text{dm}³ CO.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0203.explanation: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, PV is constant and does not change with P. On a plot of PV (y-axis) against P (x-axis), the ideal gas is a horizontal line. The horizontal line is labeled N.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0204.explanation: Graham’s law: (r_Y)/(r_Z) = √((M_Z)/(M_Y)). Given r_Y = 2r_Z: 2 = √((M_Z)/(64)). Squaring: 4 = (M_Z)/(64) so M_Z = 256. This value is not among the listed options; from the image options, the intended arrangement is typically r_Y is twice r_Z implying M_Z = 256. Because 256 is absent, the closest common exam variant is reversed ratio (if r_Z = 2r_Y then M_Z = 16). However, using the wording as shown, the computed result is 256, which is not provided.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0206.explanation: Fluorine (Z=9): 1s² 2s² 2p⁵. In the three 2p orbitals, five electrons leave one unpaired electron (Hund’s rule).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0207.explanation: Gamma rays are the least ionizing (though most penetrating) among the common radioactive emissions listed.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0208.explanation: CO2 has two electron regions around the carbon (two double bonds), giving a linear geometry (O=C=O).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0209.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is strongest when H is bonded to highly electronegative atoms (F, O, N). HF forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0210.explanation: The first configuration is Mg (metal) and the second is O (non-metal). Mg transfers electrons to O forming text{Mg}²⁺ and text{O}²⁻: an ionic bond.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0211.explanation: Nitrogen makes up the largest proportion of air and is relatively unreactive, so it dilutes oxygen and reduces the rate of combustion.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0213.explanation: Calcium chloride readily absorbs moisture from air and is commonly used as a drying agent (hygroscopic).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0214.explanation: 42 g of water ≈ 42 cm³ = 0.042 dm³ (density ≈ 1 g cm⁻³). Solubility in g dm⁻³ = (24.4)/(0.042) ≈ 580.95 ≈ 581.000.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0215.explanation: Grease is non-polar; turpentine is a non-polar organic solvent that dissolves grease effectively.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0216.explanation: Sewage provides nutrients for bacteria; bacterial decomposition increases BOD and consumes dissolved oxygen, lowering oxygen levels.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0217.explanation: Moles of HCl initially: n = CV = 2.0× 2.5 = 5.0 mol. Final volume: 2.5 + 10.0 = 12.5 dm³. Final concentration: C_f = (5.0)/(12.5) = 0.4 text{mol dm}⁻³.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0218.explanation: Adding HCl increases [text{H}^+], so pH decreases below 6.4.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0219.explanation: Aluminium oxide (Al2O3) is an oxide, not a salt. The others are salts (acid salt, carbonate, and chloride).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0220.explanation: Insoluble salts are commonly prepared by precipitation (double decomposition) by mixing two soluble salt solutions to form an insoluble product.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0221.explanation: Fluorine goes from oxidation state 0 in F2 to -1 in HF, so it gains electrons (is reduced).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0222.explanation: Cu2+ (in CuSO4) is reduced to Cu(s). The species reduced is the oxidizing agent, hence CuSO4.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0223.explanation: Polarization is commonly due to hydrogen gas bubbles accumulating on an electrode surface, increasing internal resistance.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0224.explanation: Charge passed: Q = It = 5× 193 = 965 text{C}. Moles of electrons: n(e^-) = (965)/(96500) = 0.010 text{mol}. For oxygen: 2text{H}₂text{O} arrow text{O}₂ + 4text{H}^+ + 4e^-, so n(text{O}₂)=(0.010)/(4)=0.0025 text{mol}. Volume at STP: V = 0.0025× 22.4 = 0.056 text{dm}³ (which is 56 cm³).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0225.explanation: Spontaneity depends on Δ G = Δ H - TΔ S. Here Δ H>0 (endothermic) and Δ S<0 (loss in entropy), so -TΔ S is positive and Δ G becomes positive: not spontaneous.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0226.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic (Δ H<0). Lowering temperature favors the exothermic direction, increasing text{SO}₃ yield.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0227.explanation: Activation energy is the minimum energy barrier that reactant particles must overcome for reaction to occur.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0228.explanation: Pure solids have activity 1 and are omitted from K. Thus K = frac{(PH_₂)⁴}{(PH_₂O)⁴} (or concentration form similarly), matching option C.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0229.explanation: CO is a neutral oxide (does not form acids or bases readily). CO2, SO2, and SO3 are acidic oxides.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0230.explanation: In ammonia preparation (heating ammonium salt with base), water forms and may condense; slanting prevents condensed liquid running back onto hot glass, which can crack the flask.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0231.explanation: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is used as an anesthetic/analgesic gas.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0232.explanation: In water, SO2 forms sulphurous acid (H2SO3) which ionizes to sulphite (trioxosulphate(IV)) species; these are readily oxidized to sulphate, so the solution behaves as a reducing agent.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0233.explanation: Alkali metal sulphites (e.g., K2SO3) are soluble in water; barium sulphite is sparingly soluble.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0234.explanation: Copper is relatively low in the reactivity (activity) series, so many metals above it can displace Cu2+ from solution.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0235.explanation: In 2-methylbutan-2-ol, the carbon bearing the OH group is attached to three carbon groups, so it is a tertiary alcohol.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0236.explanation: Ammonia reacts with an ester to give an amide and an alcohol. Ethyl ethanoate (CH3COOC2H5) gives ethanamide (CH3CONH2) and ethanol (C2H5OH).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0237.explanation: Decarboxylation of a carboxylic acid removes CO2 and forms an alkane with one fewer carbon. Ethanoic acid (2 carbons) gives methane (1 carbon).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0238.explanation: The drawn structure shows a carbonyl group (C=O) on a non-terminal carbon (ketone position), which corresponds to an alkanone.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0239.explanation: NaOH neutralizes carboxylic acids to form a salt and water. Propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH) reacts to form sodium propanoate and water.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0240.explanation: Amines (RNH2) are basic in water and turn red litmus paper blue.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0241.explanation: Heating (dehydrating) an ammonium carboxylate leads to formation of an amide: text{RCOO}^-text{NH}₄^+ arrow text{RCONH}₂ + text{H}₂text{O}.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0242.explanation: Heavier petroleum fractions are used as feedstock for cracking to produce lighter fuels; lubricating oil is a suitable heavy fraction compared with kerosene/diesel (already lighter) and bitumen (residue).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0243.explanation: Many esters (RCOOR') have pleasant fruity smells; their general formula matches option C.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0244.explanation: A primary amide has the group -text{CONH}₂, i.e., RCONH2.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0245.explanation: Longest chain including the double bond has 5 carbons. Number from the end nearest the double bond so the alkene is at C1: pent-1-ene. The branch is a methyl on carbon 2, giving 2-methylpent-1-ene.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0246.explanation: Assume 100 g: moles C = (60)/(12)=5, H = (13.3)/(1)=13.3, O = (26.7)/(16)=1.66875. Divide by 1.66875: C ≈ 3, H ≈ 8, O =1. Empirical formula: text{C}₃text{H}₈text{O}.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0248.explanation: Sand is insoluble, so it is removed by filtration. The filtrate contains water and methanoic acid (miscible liquids), so distillation separates and collects the water as the distillate.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0249.explanation: Dry gas pressure: P₁ = 765 - 5 = 760 text{mmHg}. At STP, P₂ = 760 text{mmHg}, T₂ = 273 text{K}. Also T₁ = 10 + 273 = 283 text{K}. Using (P₁V₁)/(T₁)=(P₂V₂)/(T₂) and P₁=P₂: V₂ = V₁(T₂)/(T₁) = 50×(273)/(283) ≈ 48.23 text{cm}³.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0250.explanation: At constant temperature, increasing pressure compresses a gas so its volume decreases (Boyle’s law).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0251.explanation: Volume ratios follow coefficients: text{H}₂:text{O}₂ = 2:1. For 300 cm³ text{O}₂, required text{H}₂ is 2× 300 = 600 cm³. Leftover text{H}₂ = 1000-600 = 400 cm³.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0252.explanation: All four phenomena depend on matter being made of particles in constant motion (especially diffusion and Brownian motion).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0253.explanation: Atomic number 11 is Na (metal) and 17 is Cl (non-metal). Electron transfer forms text{Na}^+ and text{Cl}^-, i.e., an ionic bond.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0254.explanation: A neutral hydrogen atom (protium) is 1 proton + 1 electron. Losing the electron leaves text{H}^+, which is just one proton.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0255.explanation: Neutral Mg (Z = 12): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s². text{Mg}²⁺ loses the two 3s electrons, leaving 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0256.explanation: Halogens (Group VII/17) readily gain electrons, so they oxidize other substances (they are oxidizing agents).

jamb-chemistry-bank-0257.explanation: Crystal structures are determined using X-ray diffraction.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0258.explanation: Air has variable composition, can be separated physically (e.g., fractionation of liquid air), and contains inert noble gases mixed with other gases—features of a mixture.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0259.explanation: Hardness is due to text{Ca}²⁺ and text{Mg}²⁺. Adding soluble sodium salts like text{Na}₂text{CO}₃ supplies text{CO}₃²⁻ to form insoluble precipitates (e.g., text{CaCO}₃), removing the ions.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0260.explanation: Chlorine disinfects water by killing harmful microorganisms.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0001.explanation: Carbon has 6 protons, giving it an atomic number of 6.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0003.explanation: At 25°C, a neutral solution has equal concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻, giving pH = 7.

jamb-chemistry-bank-0004.explanation: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑. Hydrogen gas is liberated.
